quickAnswer: Nationally, lobby marble honing and sealing runs about $1.75-$4.50 per sq ft, and terrazzo honing, polishing, and sealing runs about $2.25-$6.50 per sq ft depending on scratch depth and grit sequence. Seal-only refresh visits cost $0.45-$1.25 per sq ft, specialty stone crews bill $55-$95 per technician hour, and most vendors enforce a $450-$900 job minimum regardless of area.

blocks.text: How Stone Vendors Build a Lobby Honing and Sealing Unit Price

Marble and terrazzo restoration is not priced like nightly janitorial work. Your routine cleaning contract might sit at $0.07-$0.15 per sq ft per visit, but stone honing is a project trade billed per square foot of finished floor, and the unit price is mostly a function of how many diamond grit passes the floor needs. A light-traffic lobby with dull spots may only need a 400-800-1500 grit hone followed by a polish and penetrating sealer. A 20-year-old terrazzo entrance with etched walk lanes, lippage at divider strips, and old topical coatings can need a coating strip plus a 100-200-400-800-1500-3000 sequence before any sealer goes down.

Each grit pass costs roughly $0.30-$0.75 per sq ft in labor, diamond wear, water management, and slurry extraction. That is why two quotes for the same 3,000 sq ft lobby can differ by thousands of dollars: one vendor quoted a polish-and-seal, the other quoted a true restoration. Always ask for the starting grit and the number of passes in writing.

blocks.text: Stair treads, risers, and elevator thresholds are usually priced per piece rather than per square foot because the machine work is hand-held. Expect $35-$85 per tread for hone and seal, and $40-$120 per elevator threshold, depending on edge profile and whether bullnose polishing is required.
Worked Example: 2,800 sq ft Lobby and Elevator Bank

Consider a suburban Class B office with a 2,800 sq ft marble lobby, a 400 sq ft terrazzo vestibule, 14 stair treads, and 4 elevator thresholds. The marble has visible walk-lane dulling and coffee etches but no deep scratches; the terrazzo has an old acrylic finish that has yellowed.

blocks.text: Spread over a 24-month restoration cycle, that project amortizes to about $543 per month, or roughly $0.17 per sq ft of stone per month. Compare that against your nightly janitorial base: if a 25,000 sq ft building pays $0.05-$0.10 per sq ft per visit at 21.65 visits per month, the stone program is a small but visible line item that protects the most photographed floor in the building.

blocks.title: Benchmark check: productivity drives the rate
blocks.text: A two-person stone crew with a 20-inch planetary machine typically finishes 600-1,200 sq ft per night on a full hone and seal, versus 1,500-2,500 sq ft for a polish-and-seal only. If a vendor quotes a 3,000 sq ft full restoration in one shift, ask how many grit passes they actually plan to run.
When Hourly Billing Beats a Per-Sq-Ft Quote

Hourly billing at $55-$95 per technician hour makes sense for areas under about 300 sq ft, isolated etch repairs in front of a reception desk, or spot work around a fountain or planter. Once the area exceeds the vendor's minimum charge, per-square-foot pricing almost always protects you better because the vendor owns the productivity risk. Use hourly pricing only with a not-to-exceed cap.

items: Under 300 sq ft: hourly with a not-to-exceed cap, or simply pay the job minimum.
300-1,500 sq ft: per-sq-ft quote, expect the upper half of each range because mobilization is spread across fewer feet.
1,500-10,000 sq ft: per-sq-ft quote with defined grit sequence, sealer brand, and number of coats.
Over 10,000 sq ft (atriums, multi-floor terrazzo corridors): negotiate phased pricing and a lower unit rate for repeat nights.

blocks.text: Daily Care That Stretches the Restoration Cycle

Most lobby stone damage is grit abrasion and acid etching, both of which your nightly janitorial crew controls. Walk-off matting at least 12-15 feet deep, daily dust mopping, and neutral pH cleaners keep the hone from wearing back to dull in months. A cordless compact scrubber such as the Tennant i-mop Lite, with its 14.5-inch path and 0.8 gal tank, lets the nightly crew scrub elevator landings without flooding grout joints. For daytime grit pickup in a busy lobby, a quiet mechanical sweeper like the Rubbermaid Commercial 421288 dual-rotor unit removes sand without cords or noise near reception.

Avoid having the janitorial vendor run a high-speed burnisher on stone unless they are using diamond-impregnated or stone-specific pads. A 2000 RPM burnisher such as the Powr-Flite P202-3 is excellent for VCT finish, but on marble it should only be used with the pad system your stone vendor approves, otherwise heat and abrasive pads can haze the polish.

blocks.title: Watch the chemistry
blocks.text: Acidic restroom cleaners, vinegar, and citrus degreasers etch calcite marble within seconds. Require neutral pH cleaners in the scope, keep Safety Data Sheets on site under OSHA HazCom, and label secondary spray bottles. Etch repair is billable work your contract should not create.
What to Put in Your Stone Restoration Scope

items.name: Measure and map
items.text: Separate marble, terrazzo, stair treads, and thresholds on a floor plan so each is priced by its own unit.

items.name: Specify the grit sequence
items.text: Require the starting grit, finishing grit, and number of passes for each surface type.

items.name: Name the sealer
items.text: List the impregnating sealer, number of coats, and cure time before foot traffic resumes.

items.name: Define protection
items.text: Require masking of baseboards, elevator door tracks, and wood millwork, plus slurry containment and disposal.

items.name: Set acceptance
items.text: Agree on a gloss-meter target or walk-through standard and a 30-day touch-up window.

faqs.q: Why is a terrazzo quote often higher per sq ft than marble?
faqs.a: Older terrazzo frequently carries layers of acrylic or urethane finish that must be stripped before diamonds can cut the surface, and divider strips create lippage that requires coarse grinding. That adds one to three grit passes, which typically adds $1.00-$2.00 per sq ft compared with an uncoated marble floor of similar wear.

faqs.q: What insurance should a stone restoration vendor carry?
faqs.a: Ask for a certificate of insurance naming the building owner and property manager as additional insureds, with at least $1 million per occurrence general liability, workers compensation, and auto coverage for the equipment trailer. Water slurry can damage elevator pits and lower-floor ceilings, so confirm the policy does not exclude water damage from wet grinding operations.

faqs.q: Is a minimum charge negotiable for small lobbies?
faqs.a: Sometimes. Vendors set $450-$900 minimums to cover trailer mobilization, wet vacuums, and slurry disposal. You can often reduce the effective cost by bundling the lobby with stair treads, restroom thresholds, or a second building on the same night, so the mobilization covers more billable footage.

faqs.q: How does this compare with the monthly janitorial contract cost?
faqs.a: Nightly janitorial for a 2,500-9,999 sq ft office runs $0.09-$0.15 per sq ft per visit, multiplied by visits per month (for example 21.65 visits at five nights a week, based on 4.333 weeks per month). Stone restoration is a periodic project, so amortize it across its cycle, often 12-36 months, and show it as a separate capital-like maintenance line rather than burying it in the monthly retainer.

Many LEED or Green Seal managed buildings require low-VOC or water-based impregnating sealers and documentation of product SDS. Ask the vendor to submit the sealer's VOC content and SDS before work, and confirm the cure time so HVAC can be scheduled to ventilate the lobby overnight.
